content.text:
Nature and science facts about eagles

The eagle has some of the sharpest eyesight of any animal, spotting prey on the ground from high in the sky. When it spreads its broad wings and rides a warm thermal updraft, it can stay aloft for a long time without a single flap. It grips prey with its hooked beak and powerful talons, and builds a big nest on high cliffs or in tall trees to raise its young. Because of its majestic presence, it has been seen as a symbol of bravery in many countries.

Point out its amazing eyesight, thermal updrafts (flying without flapping), its hooked beak and talons, and its high nest. Talking together about "Why can an eagle fly without flapping its wings?" is a wonderful way to spark curiosity.

Parent guide — how to nurture curiosity

Float a piece of paper to illustrate "it stays aloft riding warm air (a thermal updraft)." Comparing how an eagle's eyes are far better than ours through a game of spotting far-off letters makes it fascinating.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Why can an eagle fly without flapping its wings?
A. Because it rides warm thermal updrafts on its wide wings. That's how it can stay aloft for a long time.

Q. How good is an eagle's eyesight?
A. It's among the sharpest of any animal — it can clearly see prey on the ground even from very high up.

Q. How can we observe eagles at home?
A. Float a piece of paper to illustrate thermal updrafts, and play an eyesight game spotting far-off letters.
